reads.title: What the Media Is Pushing on Gender This Week, Measured
reads.subtitle: Twenty topics, a week of coverage, every outlet counted. The loud stories have villains; the quiet ones have numbers.
reads.body:
THE SHORT VERSION
The desk searched twenty gender topics across a week of news, counted every outlet that carried each one and sorted them by which side of the media they sit on. The result is a map of what is being pushed and what is being left alone. The loudest gender story in America this week is a single campus case. The quietest are the ones with the most people in them.

HOW THE MEASURE WORKS
A story covered by left, centre and right outlets alike is news: everyone agrees it happened and matters. A story carried mostly by one side is a push: one audience is being sold it. A story nobody carries is the negative space, often the most useful finding, because absence is a choice too. The desk counted distinct outlets per topic from Google News over seven days and placed known outlets on a coarse political map. It is a rough instrument, and the conclusions below stay inside what it can show.

WHAT IS BEING PUSHED HARDEST
The Epstein files: 81 outlets. A federal judge ordered the Justice Department on 30 September to fast-track records mentioning President Trump and Mar-a-Lago, and Norway's parliament is questioning 11 officials over Epstein contacts. Coverage runs across the spectrum, but the framing splits: Democrats use the files against Trump, and fact-checkers are already flagging misleading ads.

Domestic violence: 85 outlets, but almost all local, because October is Domestic Violence Awareness Month. Volume without a national story is a calendar effect, not a campaign.

Cornell 7: 58 outlets in a week, and the national desks own it: The New York Times, CNN, CBS with an "exclusive" of the fraternity's group chat, ABC and PBS. Opinion writers have turned it into a referendum: Robert Reich's column is headlined "Cornell, Rape, and Misogyny in the Age of Trump." One campus case is carrying the weight of a national argument.

Trans policy: 61 outlets, both sides, driven by real decisions: the administration asking the Supreme Court to let it deny hormones to transgender prisoners, and ballot measures on girls' sports in Colorado and Washington.

Abortion: 77 outlets and steady, driven by court fights over pills mailed across state lines.

WHAT IS BEING SOLD AS A TREND
Mothers killing children: 28 outlets, almost all crime reporting on individual cases, with partisan headlines stringing them together. One detail deserves attention: a California woman charged this week was reported as "invested" in the Lindsay Clancy trial. Researchers have documented copycat effects in mass shootings and suicides when coverage is heavy; nobody has shown it for filicide, but a news cycle that turns one trial into a genre is the condition under which it would happen.

Tradwives: 19 outlets, and the trend has turned. The new story is women leaving it, "de-tradding," and outlets covering the influencers who sold it. The trend cycle now covers its own collapse.

WHAT IS NOT BEING COVERED
The 4B movement, last year's sensation about women swearing off men: one item, from a Pakistani television site. It was never large in America; the coverage was the movement.

Women losing jobs as diversity programmes are cut: one item, from a Kenyan paper. Male loneliness: six items, mostly a basketball player's partnership with a dating app. Men's suicide: 47 outlets, but local health reporting, not national framing, although men die by suicide at about four times the rate of women.

THE PATTERN
The stories with villains travel. A named fraternity, a named mother, a named billionaire. The stories with numbers and no villain, such as men's suicide, women's job losses and marriage decline, stay local or vanish. That is not a plot; it is the economics described in the desk's piece on the gender war. Anger travels, statistics do not.

THE CONSPIRACY LENS
Is someone coordinating which gender stories you see? The evidence this week says no central hand: the coverage follows court dates, awareness months and lawsuits, the ordinary drivers of news. What is coordinated is the framing inside each camp, where the same headline shapes appear across allied outlets within hours. That is a shared incentive, not a shared plan, and the desk grades the "coordinated media agenda on gender" claim as unsupported this week.

THE DESK'S CALL
Cornell 7 remains the most-covered single gender story in American national outlets through 31 October 2026. 70 percent.

WHAT WOULD CHANGE THE DESK'S MIND
Identical wording appearing across unaffiliated outlets on the same day, the fingerprint of a press release or an influence operation rather than a shared incentive. The scan will look for it next week.

SOURCES

reads.title: The Epstein Files: What the Conspiracy Gets Right, and Where It Stops
reads.subtitle: The documented core is so strong that the unproven parts ride on it. The desk grades the bundle.
reads.body:
THE SHORT VERSION
The Epstein story is the one conspiracy theory most Americans across both parties believe in some form, and parts of it are true: a rich man trafficked girls, powerful friends flew on his plane, his co-conspirator is in prison, and the government handled his case and his death badly. This week a judge ordered the Justice Department to speed up records that mention President Trump. The lens is useful here because the documented core is so strong that the unproven parts ride on it.

THE CLAIM, IN PIECES
The popular version bundles at least five claims. One: Epstein trafficked girls to powerful men. Two: there is a "client list." Three: he worked for an intelligence service. Four: he was murdered. Five: the government is protecting the people named in the files. The desk grades each, because a bundle that mixes proven and unproven claims is how true stories become unfalsifiable ones.

THE RECORD
Epstein pleaded guilty in Florida in 2008 to soliciting a minor under a plea deal later found to have broken victims' rights law. He was arrested in 2019 on federal sex-trafficking charges and died in a Manhattan jail cell weeks later; the medical examiner ruled it suicide, and the two guards on duty were charged with falsifying records and later given deferred prosecution. Ghislaine Maxwell was convicted in 2021 of sex trafficking. In July 2025 the Justice Department and the FBI said they found no incriminating "client list" and reaffirmed the suicide finding. That statement detonated a revolt inside the President's own base.

This week: on 30 September Judge Colleen Kollar-Kotelly ordered expedited processing of Freedom of Information requests for records mentioning Trump, Mar-a-Lago and senior officials including Attorney General Pam Bondi and FBI Director Kash Patel. Expedited processing is not release; it moves the requests up the queue. In Norway, parliament is questioning 11 current and former officials about Epstein contacts. A professor is presenting findings that question the suicide ruling.

GRADING THE BUNDLE
Trafficking girls, with powerful acquaintances: proven, by convictions and court records. A literal client list: unsupported; the Justice Department says none exists, and the evidence released so far is contact books, flight logs and correspondence, which show who knew him, not who committed crimes. Intelligence work: unproven. The strongest public claim is a 2019 report that the prosecutor behind the 2008 deal said he was told Epstein "belonged to intelligence"; that prosecutor, Alexander Acosta, has since said he had no knowledge of any intelligence tie. Murder: unproven but not unreasonable to ask, given broken cameras, falsified logs and a death in the most secure jail in New York; the evidence that exists supports suicide amid gross negligence. Protection of the named: partly supported, in the narrow sense that every administration has released less than it promised.

WHO SPREADS WHAT
The scan counted 81 outlets this week, the biggest gender-adjacent story of all, carried by every side. The use differs. Democrats now treat the files as a weapon against Trump; FactCheck.org flagged a Democratic ad this week for misleadingly tying Senator Susan Collins to Epstein. Parts of the right that once pushed the files now find them awkward. The story's politics flipped and the audience kept following, which tells you the demand is for the theory, not for a party.

WHAT IT FREES UP
For both parties, a scandal that can be aimed. For the public, a story that confirms a deeper suspicion that elites protect each other, which is easier to believe than the plainer truth: that a wealthy predator bought a lenient deal in 2008 and the system did not look again for a decade. For the victims, a risk: when the story becomes about politicians, it stops being about them.

THE DESK'S CALL
The Justice Department releases at least some records responsive to the expedited Trump and Mar-a-Lago requests, with redactions, by 31 December 2026. 55 percent.

WHAT WOULD CHANGE THE DESK'S MIND
A released record showing a named person paying for or arranging abuse would move "protection of the named" from partly supported to proven. A forensic finding that contradicts the suicide ruling would reopen the murder claim.

SOURCES

Expedited FOIA order (Democracy Defenders Fund): https://www.democracydefendersfund.org/news/judge-grants-expedited-processing-of-foia-request-for-epstein-files-mentioning-trump-or-mar-a-lago/

reads.title: Andrew Tate in an American Jail: The Martyr Machine
reads.subtitle: Charged by Britain, arrested in Miami, and sold to his followers as a political prisoner.
reads.body:
THE SHORT VERSION
Andrew Tate, the most famous man in the online manosphere, is in an American jail. He and his brother Tristan were arrested in Miami in July on British charges and are fighting extradition to England. His followers say he is a political prisoner of "the Matrix." The record says he faces some of the most serious sex-crime charges an influencer has ever faced, in a country he chose to fly to.

THE CLAIM
Tate's world has a story ready for everything: that he is persecuted for telling young men the truth, that governments and banks ("the Matrix") want him silenced, and that every charge is part of the attack. The story turns legal trouble into proof of importance, and it is told by thousands of paid members of his online school, who earn commission for every recruit and are encouraged to post his clips.

THE RECORD
On 18 July 2026 the Tate brothers were arrested in Miami after British prosecutors brought new charges. Andrew Tate faces seven further counts of rape, three of arranging trafficking for sexual exploitation, three of assault causing bodily harm, and 19 charges over indecent images of a child and extreme pornography. Tristan faces rape, sexual assault and trafficking counts. The new charges relate to four more women and came from Bedfordshire Police in England. Both deny everything.

They were already wanted. Romania charged them in 2023 with trafficking and forming a criminal gang; that case was sent back over procedure. In early 2025 Romania let them fly to Florida, after the Financial Times reported that Richard Grenell, a Trump envoy, raised them with Romania's foreign minister. A US court will now decide whether to send them to Britain.

Meanwhile the money keeps moving. Financial sites report large transfers from wallets linked to Tate, including nearly $1.9 million in one cryptocurrency, while he sits in jail.

WHO SPREADS WHAT
The scan found 20 outlets covering Tate this week, but the mainstream barely touched him: one centre outlet, zero on the left or right. Most of the coverage was crypto and finance sites tracking his wallets, plus true-crime explainers. His own network carries the persecution story; the press has mostly moved on. That gap matters: a figure who is ignored by the press and amplified by his own paid network reaches young men without any counter-story in the same feed.

THE COUNTER
Persecution stories have one weakness: evidence in a courtroom. Britain's charges came from police in England, not from any American political fight, and extradition hearings test whether the paperwork and the evidence meet the treaty's standard, not whether the defendant is popular. If the British case is weak, it will fail in an English court under English rules of evidence, which is the arena his followers say he wants.

THE DESK'S READ
The claim that he is a political prisoner: unsupported. He was charged by British prosecutors on evidence from British police, and arrested in a country that let him in. The claim that powerful people helped him before: partly supported, since the reported Grenell intervention is on the record. The claim that his influence on boys is overstated: contradicted by the University of Kent and UCL study that watched a teenage boy's TikTok feed go from 13 to 56 percent misogynistic content in five days.

WHAT IT FREES UP
For his business, martyrdom sells subscriptions. For the wider manosphere, a jailed leader is a recruitment story. For his critics, a conviction would be proof the content was always a front. Each side already knows how it will tell the ending.

THE DESK'S CALL
A US magistrate certifies the brothers as extraditable to the UK by 30 June 2027. 60 percent.

WHAT WOULD CHANGE THE DESK'S MIND
Britain withdrawing or reducing the charges before the hearing would support the persecution story; a certification followed by an English trial would end it.

reads.title: Feminism Was a CIA Plot, Tradwives Are a Psyop: Two Mirror Conspiracies
reads.subtitle: Both start from real money and power. Both take away women's agency to make a point about their enemies.
reads.body:
THE SHORT VERSION
Two conspiracy theories about women's lives are running at the same time, and they are mirror images. On the right: feminism was a CIA operation. On the left: tradwives are a psychological operation to push women back into the home. Both start from something real, and both claim far more than the record holds. Reading them together is the best lesson in the conspiracy lens the desk can offer.

THE FIRST CLAIM: FEMINISM WAS A CIA PROJECT
The story says the CIA created or steered the women's movement, usually through Gloria Steinem, to break up the family, put women into the taxable workforce and divide the left.

What is true: from about 1959 to 1962 Steinem ran the Independent Research Service, which was funded almost entirely by the CIA to send non-communist American students to Soviet-sponsored youth festivals in Vienna and Helsinki. When Ramparts magazine exposed the CIA's student funding in 1967, Steinem confirmed it publicly to The New York Times and The Washington Post. The CIA's own history describes a strategy of "promoting the non-Communist left," funding magazines, unions and student groups that could compete with communism from inside progressive politics.

What is not shown: any CIA role in founding Ms. magazine, writing the movement's demands or directing second-wave feminism. The CIA funded many anti-communist cultural fronts in the 1950s; that it touched a young Steinem a decade before the women's movement peaked shows it recruited bright young progressives, not that it invented their later causes. Grade: the connection, proven; the operation, unsupported.

THE SECOND CLAIM: TRADWIVES ARE A PSYOP
The story says the explosion of "traditional wife" influencers, women baking bread from scratch and serving husbands on camera, is a coordinated campaign by conservatives, billionaires or foreign states to talk young women out of careers and into motherhood.

What is true: the tradwife boom was a business, and political networks loved it. The biggest accounts earned brand deals and product lines; Jezebel this month called one star someone who "profits off pretending" to be a tradwife. Pronatalist activists and parts of the Trump coalition promote the same ideal, and the administration has floated baby bonuses and a "motherhood medal" for women with six children. The scan also found the trend reversing: this week's coverage is about women quitting it, "de-tradding," and about Gen Z couples rushing to marry under a tradwife-era makeover of the old "ring by spring" campus tradition.

What is not shown: a coordinating hand. The accounts grew because the algorithm rewards aspirational domestic content, the same way it rewards luxury travel; their audiences are often women who watch them the way people watch cooking shows, without wanting the life. Grade: political promotion of the ideal, supported; a manufactured psyop, unsupported.

THE MIRROR
Each theory does the same three things. It finds a real thread of money or power: CIA cheques in the 1950s, brand deals and pronatalist conferences now. It skips the middle step of showing that the money directed the outcome. And it explains a huge, organic social change, women entering work or some women choosing home, as something done to women rather than chosen by them. That last move is the tell. Both theories take away women's agency in order to make a point about their enemies.

WHAT EACH ONE FREES UP
The CIA story lets opponents of feminism call it foreign and fake without arguing with its demands. The psyop story lets critics of tradwives dismiss the women who like the content instead of asking why a hard economy makes a home-centred life look appealing. Both save their believers an argument.

THE DESK'S READ
Real threads, overreaching conclusions, and a shared habit of treating women as targets rather than actors. Follow the money to the edge of what it proves, and stop there.

WHAT WOULD CHANGE THE DESK'S MIND
For the first claim: a declassified CIA record tasking officers to shape the women's movement's agenda after 1965. For the second: evidence that the largest tradwife accounts were paid by a political organisation or a state, the way Russian operations paid for divisive accounts in 2016.

SOURCES

reads.title: Who Wants You to Have Babies
reads.subtitle: A movement with friends in the White House, critics who call it control, and a birth rate no government has bought back.
reads.body:
THE SHORT VERSION
A movement wants Americans to have more babies, and for the first time it has friends in the White House: the Vice President, the world's richest man and a network of conferences and think tanks. Its critics say it is about control of women. Its fringe says the falling birth rate was engineered. The record supports a simpler and more interesting story: birth rates are falling across almost every rich country, governments are trying to buy them back, and nothing has worked very well.

WHAT IS HAPPENING
Births are falling everywhere money is. This week Singapore, which has one of the lowest fertility rates on earth, launched a government-run dating app for its civil servants. China is turning empty schools into care homes for the elderly. Mexico's Yucatán has one of its country's lowest birth rates. The New York Times asked this week whether cheaper housing could reverse the decline.

In the United States, the administration's tax law gives every baby born a citizen from July 2026 a $1,000 "Trump account," a savings account seeded by the government. Officials have also floated a $5,000 baby bonus, a "motherhood medal" for women with six or more children, and reserving 30 percent of Fulbright scholarships for applicants who are married or have children. The "motherhood medal" idea was helped along by Simone Collins, who with her husband Malcolm runs one of the movement's best-known families. Elon Musk, father of at least 14 children, calls population collapse a bigger risk than climate change. The movement meets at an annual conference in Austin called NatalCon.

THE CLAIMS
From critics: pronatalism is "pro-control, not pro-baby," a programme to push women out of public life, linked to the "Great Replacement" fear that white populations are being outbred. From the fringe right: falling births were caused on purpose, by birth control, feminism, chemicals or elites who want a smaller, more dependent population.

GRADING
That the movement has influence in the administration: supported. The baby account is law, and the proposals came from people with access. That it is mainly about controlling women: partly supported. Some of its most prominent voices pair baby bonuses with opposition to abortion and with talk of traditional roles, and women's groups have documented those links; but many pronatalist policies, such as child allowances, paid leave and cheaper housing, are ones feminists have backed for decades, which is why some on the left say the right is recycling their ideas. That it is about race: supported for parts of the fringe and contested for the mainstream; the evidence is in who speaks at the conferences and what they say, and it varies widely. That the decline was engineered: unsupported. Fertility falls with wealth, education, urban living and the cost of raising children in every culture that has measured it, including countries with opposite politics to America's.

WHAT DOES NOT WORK, AND WHAT DOES
Cash bonuses raise births a little and mostly change their timing; economists expect a $1,000 account to do almost nothing to the birth rate. Countries that have spent the most, such as South Korea, still have the lowest rates. What moves fertility is slower and less political: affordable housing, childcare that lets two parents work, and confidence about the future. That is why the debate often sounds like culture war: the policies that would work cost money, and the culture war is free.

WHAT IT FREES UP
For the administration, a family-values message that costs $1,000 a baby. For the tech pronatalists, a moral story for a world they want more people in. For critics, a way to tie the movement to its worst members. For everyone, a way to avoid the cost of housing.

THE DESK'S CALL
No federal cash baby bonus of $5,000 or more becomes law by 31 December 2027. 80 percent.

WHAT WOULD CHANGE THE DESK'S MIND
A US birth rate that rises for two straight years after the Trump accounts begin, with no change in housing or childcare costs, would show money alone can move it.

SOURCES
Pronatalism and the Trump administration (Population Connection): https://populationconnection.org/learn/pronatalism-in-the-us/
Critics' report (National Women's Law Center): https://nwlc.org/press-release/behind-the-baby-bonuses-new-report-argues-pronatalism-is-pro-control-not-pro-baby/
Why a baby bonus is unlikely to raise fertility (Yahoo News): https://www.yahoo.com/news/why-trump-baby-bonus-unlikely-100000546.html

Pronatalism explained (OPB): https://www.opb.org/article/2025/04/25/what-is-pronatalism-and-what-role-do-musk-and-vance-have-with-it/

reads.title: The Gender War Is a Product
reads.subtitle: The split between young men and women is real. The war on top of it is manufactured, and here is who makes it.
reads.body:
THE SHORT VERSION
There is a real split between young men and young women in America. There is also a gender war, and the war is mostly a product: something platforms, outlets, influencers and campaigns make, because conflict between the sexes is the cheapest attention on the internet. The split is data. The war is packaging. This piece separates the two.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY ON THE RECORD
Young women moved left. Gallup found 40 percent of women aged 18 to 29 called themselves liberal in 2017 to 2024, up from 28 percent in 2001 to 2007. Young men barely moved: 25 percent liberal, against 27 percent in the decade before. The gap opened because one group moved, not because both ran to opposite corners.

Then it showed up at the ballot box. In AP VoteCast, the Associated Press's survey of voters, men under 30 backed Trump 56 to 42 in 2024 and women under 30 backed Harris 58 to 41. The youth gender gap went from 17 points in 2020 to 31.

That is the real material. Everything below is about what gets built on top of it.

THE MACHINE, PART ONE: ANGER IS WHAT GETS SHARED
In 2021 three researchers (Rathje, Van Bavel and van der Linden) measured millions of posts and found that language about the other side was the single strongest predictor of a post being shared. Stronger than emotional language. Each extra word about the other side raised the odds of a share by about two thirds. A post saying "women are doing X to kids" or "men are doing X to women" is built to that spec.

Then the platforms pay for it. Since November 2024, X has paid creators by how much its paying subscribers engage with their posts, not by advertising. Engagement is the product, and out-group anger is the most reliable way to make it. Nobody needs to plan a gender war for it to pay.

THE MACHINE, PART TWO: THE FEED FINDS THE VULNERABLE
The University of Kent and University College London built test accounts modelled on real teenage boys and watched TikTok's recommendation feed. On day one, 13 percent of recommended videos were misogynistic. By day five it was 56 percent: a fourfold rise in five days, with nobody searching for it. The researchers found the feed targets loneliness and a feeling of lost control, which is a description of a large share of teenage boys.

The same mechanism runs the other way. After the 2024 election, Google searches for 4B, a fringe South Korean movement of women swearing off men, jumped by hundreds of percent, and national outlets ran explainers for a week. A movement with almost no American members became a headline because it fit the war story.

THE MACHINE, PART THREE: PEOPLE WHO SELL IT
Andrew Tate's online school, The Real World, charges $49 a month and claims more than 200,000 paying members. Members earned 45 to 50 percent commission for every recruit, and were told to flood TikTok, YouTube Shorts and Instagram with clips of Tate. That is a distribution network paid in commissions: the outrage is the marketing, and the subscription is the business.

Campaigns read the same map. Trump appeared on more than a dozen podcasts with mostly male audiences in 2024, reportedly with his son Barron advising on which. The Joe Rogan interview passed 50 million views on YouTube alone, and Trump reached about 25 times more viewers than Harris in that medium. The other party now holds meetings about how to win men back. Both are treating the sexes as two separate markets, and campaigns spend money only where they think it moves votes.

THE MACHINE, PART FOUR: THE SWARM AND THE STATE
In 2022, during the Johnny Depp and Amber Heard trial, the monitoring firm Bot Sentinel found 627 accounts devoted to attacking Heard and the women who defended her, a quarter of them created in the previous seven months, using copy-and-paste tactics to game the trending lists. A real trial, real testimony, and a pile-on that was partly manufactured. That is the precedent for every gender-coded court case since, Cornell 7 included.

States use the wedge too. Research at Queen's University in Canada documents Russian state accounts spreading posts that call feminists man-hating, while also posing as feminists to split them from each other. The goal is not a view on women. It is a divided public that trusts nobody.

HOW TODAY'S STORIES GET USED
This week supplied raw material for both sides. On the right, two mothers' child-killing cases in one week became "Another Murdering Mom?", a trend story with no trend under it: since 1976, fathers and mothers have killed young children at about the same rate. On the left, the Cornell 7 case, a disputed rape allegation now under a special prosecutor, is treated as proof about men in general. Then the two get paired: men are charged on thin evidence while mothers who kill walk free. Each piece has a fact in it; the pairing is the propaganda.

WHAT THE WAR FREES UP
Ask what this frees up for the people running it. For platforms, guaranteed engagement. For influencers, subscribers. For campaigns, a turnout engine that needs no policy. For foreign services, a divided rival at no cost. And for everyone, a way to avoid the harder questions: young men falling behind in college, pay and friendship; young women losing ground on reproductive rights and safety. Those problems are real, measurable and fixable. A war is easier to sell.

DESIGN OR DRIFT
Mostly drift. No central office runs the gender war. It is what happens when every actor takes their cheapest option inside an attention economy that pays for anger. There are designed nodes inside it: Tate's affiliate scheme, the 2024 podcast strategy, the Heard swarm, Russian operations. Calling the whole thing a plot overstates it; calling it organic understates the money.

THE DESK'S CALL
By 31 December 2026, the special prosecutor's decision on Cornell 7, whichever way it goes, will be framed by the largest partisan outlets on both sides as a verdict on men or on women, not on the evidence. 85 percent.

WHAT WOULD CHANGE THE DESK'S MIND
If surveys away from social media, such as Gallup or the American Survey Center, found that most young men and young women personally see the other sex as an opponent, the war would be real and not a product. Today they show different politics, not mutual hostility.

reads.title: "Women Are Killing Kids": A Trend That Isn't
reads.subtitle: Two horrifying cases in one week, and a headline that counted to two.
reads.body:
THE SHORT VERSION
Two mothers' child-killing cases landed in the same week, and parts of the media turned them into a trend: women are killing kids. The cases are real and horrifying. The trend is not. Mothers and fathers have killed their children at about the same rate for as long as the government has counted, and nothing in the data shows a rise.

WHAT HAPPENED THIS WEEK
On 1 October a Massachusetts judge refused to acquit Lindsay Clancy, who is accused of strangling her three children in 2023 and argues postpartum psychosis, a severe mental illness that can follow childbirth. Her first jury could not agree on a verdict. On 2 October a Texas mother was charged with capital murder in the shooting of her two sons. RedState ran the second story under the headline "Another Murdering Mom?", and Western Journal called the Clancy ruling what "we're all thinking."

THE NUMBER THAT DOES NOT MOVE
The Bureau of Justice Statistics, the Justice Department's data office, tracked murdered children under five from 1976 to 2005: fathers killed 31 percent, mothers 29 percent. Mothers account for more killings of newborns and infants, often tied to mental illness and isolation; fathers for more killings of older children, and far more often kill themselves afterwards. A 2026 review in the psychiatric journal Focus reached the same answer: parents of both sexes kill their children at similar rates.

So the honest headline is grim but not new: in a country of 330 million people, a few hundred children a year are killed by a parent, and the parent is about as likely to be a father as a mother.

WHY IT FEELS LIKE A TREND
Three things make two cases look like a wave. Timing: two stories in one week read as a pattern even when the yearly count is flat. Selection: outlets choose which cases become national news, and a mother killing her children is the rarer-seeming story because it breaks a deep expectation, so it travels further than a father doing the same. Framing: "another" in a headline asserts a series without counting one.

A Substack this month listed 21 cases of parents killing children across 2025 and 2026. A list is not a rate. Without a denominator and a comparison year, it tells you what someone collected, not whether anything changed.

WHAT THE FRAME IS FOR
The frame turns individual crimes into a claim about half the population, and then pairs it with stories about men accused of crimes to argue that the system goes easy on women. There is a real fact underneath that second argument: Sonja Starr's 2012 study at the University of Michigan found men receive federal sentences about 63 percent longer than women for comparable crimes. That gap is worth arguing about with data. Saying "women are killing kids" does not argue it; it borrows its anger.

THE DESK'S READ
The cases: real, and the Clancy trial turns on whether postpartum psychosis meets the legal test for insanity, which is a narrow question for a jury, not a referendum on mothers. The trend: false on the record. The frame: an engagement play that will return with the next case, whichever sex the parent is.

WHAT WOULD CHANGE THE DESK'S MIND
FBI or Bureau of Justice Statistics data for 2025 and 2026 showing child homicides by mothers rising faster than those by fathers. The desk will check when the 2025 figures are released.

reads.title: Cornell 7: The Case, and the Proxy War Around It
reads.subtitle: A disputed allegation, a failed first look, and a fight between Albany and Trump that has little to do with either.
reads.body:
THE SHORT VERSION
Cornell 7 is a real allegation with genuinely disputed facts, now under a special prosecutor. It has also become a proxy fight between New York's Democratic leadership and President Trump. The question that matters, whether a young woman was too drugged or drunk to consent, will be answered by evidence. Almost everything you read about it this month is about something else.

THE FACTS ON THE RECORD
A Cornell sophomore, called Jane Doe in court papers, says seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity drugged her with ketamine and raped her on the night of 19 to 20 October 2024. She reported it to campus police on 8 November 2024.

The Tompkins County District Attorney, Matthew Van Houten, declined to take it to a grand jury, the panel that decides whether to bring charges. He later said he had read only a six-page summary, not the 120-page police transcript, and that the summary described her participation as voluntary.

Cornell's own Title IX process, the federal rule that obliges colleges to investigate sexual misconduct, found against some of the men in May 2025: two expelled, two suspended, two found not responsible, one already graduated. The chapter was closed.

In September 2026 she sued Cornell and the seven men. On 28 September prosecutors said they would reopen the case. On 1 October Governor Kathy Hochul removed it from Van Houten and appointed Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor.

WHAT IS DISPUTED
Her first statement to police described some of the encounters as consensual; the lawsuit says she was incapacitated throughout. The men's accounts contradict each other: one says he never touched her, one admits offensive messages but denies any sexual contact, and one, through his lawyer, describes a brief consensual encounter with no sign she was impaired. No one has been charged. New York law makes cases like this hard: when a person drinks voluntarily, prosecutors must show they were incapable of consent, not just drunk. Hochul has promised to change that law.

HOW IT BECAME A PROXY WAR
Letitia James is the attorney general who brought the civil fraud case against Trump's company. Her appointment turned a campus case into a Trump story. Trump said the seven "won't get a fair shake." Student journalists at the Cornell Daily Sun published the men's names on 26 September, before any charge. State legislators and the Ithaca mayor moved on policy. Each camp now has a stake in the outcome that is unrelated to what happened in the house that night.

The template is Depp and Heard in 2022: a real dispute between real people, turned into a referendum on men or women, with a swarm of accounts on top. Partisan audiences will judge Cornell 7 by who is prosecuting and who is complaining.

TWO NUMBERS TO HOLD AGAINST THE NOISE
Research on false reports cuts both ways and is often misquoted. David Lisak's 2010 study of ten years of reports at one large university found 5.9 percent were false, and the research he reviewed puts the range at 2 to 10 percent. That means most reports are true; it also means a report alone does not prove a specific case. At the same time, most rapes are never reported or charged, and cases involving alcohol are the least likely to reach a jury. Neither number tells you what happened at Chi Phi.

THE DESK'S READ
The allegation is serious and was handled badly at the first step: a prosecutor deciding from a summary is a failure whichever way the evidence points. The men are, in law, unaccused. The special prosecutor now owns the evidence, the text messages and any drug tests, and the only verdict worth waiting for is hers.

THE DESK'S CALL
Attorney General James announces whether she will present the case to a grand jury by 31 March 2027. 70 percent.

WHAT WOULD CHANGE THE DESK'S MIND
Toxicology or messages that settle the incapacity question one way or the other would turn this from a disputed case into a clear one; the desk would say so in either direction.
